title: Prompt optimization
summary: Optimizers search for better instructions, examples, tool descriptions or models against a metric on a dataset, so you re-tune programmatically instead of editing prompt strings by hand.
useIf: You have a trustworthy metric, a few dozen labelled cases and prompts or models that change often.
avoidIf: You have no metric or no review capacity. Without a metric there is nothing to optimize, and optimized prompts can regress on specific inputs.

explain.md: Hand tuning is slow and subjective: edit, test, repeat. A **prompt optimizer** automates the loop. You supply a dataset and a metric. The optimizer proposes candidates, scores each on the same data, ranks them and returns the best. Three families matter.

items: **DSPy** compiles declarative modules against a metric. In the paper, compiled pipelines beat standard few-shot prompting generally by over 25% with GPT-3.5 and 65% with llama2-13b-chat [[r12]]. MIPRO beat baselines on 5 of 7 programs by up to 13% with Llama-3-8B [[tr11]]. GEPA, reflective prompt evolution, beat GRPO by 6% on average and up to 20% with up to 35x fewer rollouts, and beat MIPROv2 by over 10% [[r13]]. All figures are author-reported [[r14]].

**Foundry agent optimizer** (Agent Service). For a prompt agent it can improve instructions, function-calling tool descriptions and model selection. For a hosted agent it can also improve skills [[r15]].

**OpenAI dataset-backed prompt optimizer**, deprecated with the Evals platform: read-only for existing users on 2026-10-31, shutdown scheduled for 2026-11-30. Its docs warn optimized prompts can perform worse on specific inputs and must be reviewed before production [[r11]].

explain.title: The optimizer loop and where you stay in charge
explain.alt: A dataset and metric feed candidate generation. Candidates are scored and ranked, then a human review and a held-out check gate the release.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  D[Dataset and metric] --> G[Generate candidates]
  G --> E[Score on dataset]
  E --> R[Rank]
  R --> H[Review and held-out check]
  H --> P[Release via eval gate]
  H -.->|reject| G

explain.md: In the Foundry optimizer an eval model scores responses and an optimization model proposes candidates. Candidates get a composite score from 0.0 to 1.0 and a prompt-agent winner can be promoted to a new agent version [[r15]]. The optimizer invokes your agent on every dataset task, so external tool calls really run. Use test endpoints or mocks. The pre-run cost estimate in the portal is modeled and is not a spending limit [[tr4]]. Treat it as preview as of 2026-10-13: the Learn page text did not state GA when checked, so verify status before relying on it.

explain.title: Optimizing the metric, not the job
explain.md: An optimizer maximises what you measure. A thin dataset or a weak LLM judge produces prompts that win the benchmark and lose on real traffic. Hold out cases the optimizer never saw.

whereToUse: Multi-step LLM programs (retrieve, reason, answer) where each module has instructions and examples to tune
Agents on Foundry Agent Service with a dataset from real traces and built-in or custom evaluators
Teams that swap models often and want to re-optimize instead of hand-porting prompts
Improving function-calling tool descriptions so the model picks the right tool

use: A metric you trust and a few dozen labelled or trace-derived cases exist
Models change often, so re-optimization saves repeated manual work
Reviewers can read the diff and a held-out set can confirm the gain
avoid: No metric: there is nothing to optimize against
Tools charge money or change state and you have no test endpoint or mocks
You need GA only and the optimizer is preview
flips: You can build a rubric and a golden set: an optimizer becomes viable
Models change quarterly instead of yearly: programmatic re-optimization beats hand tuning
Only function tools run client side: the optimizer can tune their descriptions but cannot evaluate their execution

pitfalls.symptom: Benchmark score rises but live quality falls
pitfalls.cause: The dataset is thin or unrepresentative, or the judge rewards length or style
pitfalls.fix: Build the dataset from real traces, validate the judge against human labels and keep a held-out set.

pitfalls.symptom: Optimization run triggers real side effects
pitfalls.cause: The optimizer invokes the agent on every task, so external tool calls execute
pitfalls.fix: Point tools at test endpoints or mock them. Check cost and rate limits before the run.

pitfalls.symptom: An optimized prompt is accepted without review
pitfalls.cause: The winner looks better on aggregate and nobody reads the diff
pitfalls.fix: Review the before and after text, check regressions per slice and ship through the normal eval gate.

scenarios.title: Agent with traces, mockable tools
scenarios.situation: An agent on Foundry Agent Service has run for months. You have 300 traced tasks with human-confirmed outcomes. A model change is planned next quarter. Tools can be pointed at a sandbox.
constraints: Preview features are acceptable in a staging path
unknowns: Do the evaluators agree with human labels?
How large is the cost estimate?
scenarios.question: How do you improve the instructions?

options.name: Keep hand tuning
options.tradeoff: You repeat the effort at every model change and results vary by editor.

options.name: Run the agent optimizer on a sandboxed copy with a held-out slice, then review and promote
options.why: Data, evaluators and safe tools are in place, and review plus a held-out slice guard against overfitting.
options.tradeoff: Preview feature, run cost and review time.

options.name: Run it against production tools to get realistic results
options.why: The optimizer invokes the agent on every task, so real calls would run and could charge or change state.
options.tradeoff: Only acceptable for read-only tools with no cost or rate-limit concern.

flips.if: Your policy allows GA features only
flips.then: Hand tune or use an open-source optimizer in your own pipeline.

scenarios.takeaway: Optimize only with a trusted metric, safe tools and a held-out check.

scenarios.title: Subjective tone, no metric
scenarios.situation: A marketing assistant must write in a brand voice. Reviewers disagree on what good looks like and there are only 15 examples.
unknowns: Can reviewers agree on a rubric?
scenarios.question: Do you run an optimizer?

options.name: Run DSPy on the 15 examples
options.tradeoff: Small data overfits, so expect high variance and keep a human in the loop.

options.name: Hand tune and build a rubric and a larger example set first
options.why: Without a metric an optimizer has no target, and the rubric is the asset that later enables optimization.

options.name: Optimize against an unvalidated LLM judge scoring 'brand fit'
options.why: The optimizer will overfit to the judge's biases, not to what reviewers want.
options.tradeoff: Viable after the judge is calibrated against human ratings on a held-out set.

flips.if: Reviewers converge on a rubric and 100 labelled cases exist

flips.then: Keep human review on every release.

scenarios.takeaway: No metric means no optimizer. Build the metric first.

quiz.q: Optimized prompts score higher offline but real users report worse answers. What is the best first fix?
options: Use a larger optimization model and rerun the same optimization
Rebuild the dataset from real traces and add a held-out set
quiz.explain: The usual cause is a thin or unrepresentative dataset or an over-optimized metric. A bigger optimizer model, removing the metric or raising temperature do not repair the mismatch.

quiz.q: Before running the Foundry agent optimizer, which actions are sensible?
options: Point external tools at test endpoints or mocks
Check that tool calls will not charge money or mutate state
Assume client-side function tools are executed and evaluated
Treat the pre-run cost estimate as a spending cap
quiz.explain: The optimizer invokes the agent on every dataset task, so tool calls run. Client-side function tools are not evaluated, and the estimate is modeled, not a limit.

quiz.q: What makes programmatic optimization (DSPy style) more attractive than hand tuning?
options: Models change often and you have a trusted metric
You have no labelled data and no metric to optimize against
You need zero review of the final prompt
The prompt is a single sentence
quiz.explain: Re-optimizing against a metric saves repeated manual work when models change. Without data or a metric an optimizer cannot work, and review remains necessary.

flashcards.front: What does DSPy compile modules against?
flashcards.back: A metric on a dataset. It tunes instructions and examples programmatically so you can re-optimize when the model changes.

flashcards.front: What risk does the OpenAI optimizer doc call out?
flashcards.back: Optimized prompts can perform worse on specific inputs, so they must be reviewed before production.

flashcards.front: Why must you mock tools during Foundry agent optimization?
flashcards.back: The optimizer invokes your agent on every dataset task, so external calls execute and can charge money or change state.
